questions.q: What does held-out preference accuracy measure?
options: How many parameters the reward model has
The fraction of unseen (never-trained-on) preference pairs where the reward model assigns a higher score to the chosen response than the rejected one
The speed of the reward model's forward pass
The length difference between chosen and rejected responses
questions.explain: Held-out preference accuracy directly mirrors the training objective: checking, on data the model never saw, whether chosen consistently outscores rejected.

questions.q: Why is human-human agreement a useful reference point for evaluating a reward model's accuracy?
options: Because it has no relevance to reward model evaluation
Because it gives a natural ceiling: a reward model noticeably below typical agreement between two human annotators on the same comparisons is not yet trustworthy as a human stand-in
Because human-human agreement is always 100%
Because it replaces the need for a held-out dataset entirely
questions.explain: If multiple annotators label the same comparisons, their agreement rate sets a realistic ceiling — a reward model should approach, not wildly exceed or fall far short of, that level.

questions.q: What problem can high held-out accuracy fail to reveal, which calibration checking catches?
options: Whether the model uses enough GPU memory

The model could be right most of the time while being overconfident or underconfident about which specific comparisons it's right on, so its predicted preference probability doesn't match its empirical correctness rate
Whether the tokenizer matches the base model
Whether the dataset contains duplicate prompts
questions.explain: Calibration checks whether, among comparisons where the model predicts e.g. 70% confidence, it's actually correct about 70% of the time — a distinct question from overall accuracy.

questions.q: Why is correlating reward model scores with an independent judgment source (a different judge model or annotator panel) valuable, beyond held-out accuracy from the same pipeline?
options: It is purely a formality with no diagnostic value

Held-out accuracy still comes from the same annotation pipeline and can share its blind spots; an independent source can reveal divergences that are an early warning sign for exactly what reward model overoptimization would later exploit
It replaces the need for the Bradley-Terry loss during training
It only matters after RL training has already finished
questions.explain: An independent judgment source isn't subject to the same annotation blind spots as the training data, so disagreement there surfaces risks that same-pipeline accuracy metrics can miss.

questions.q: According to this lesson, when should reward model evaluation diagnostics (accuracy, calibration, independent correlation) be run?
options: Only once, immediately after training completes, and never again
Only after RL training has fully finished and the model is being deployed
Before RL training begins as a gate, and periodically re-run during RL training itself to watch for proxy-versus-true-quality divergence
Only if the reward model's loss value is exactly zero
questions.explain: Evaluation is treated as a gate before RL optimization begins, and the same diagnostics are typically re-run during RL training to catch overoptimization as early and cheaply as possible.
